In 2017, donors gave around $9 million to fund AI safety work.

In 2025, a single funder, Coefficient Giving, gave over $400 million.[1](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-1) In 2026, it plans to spend [over $1 billion](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/B6d8Wzk4gNzHsXvdi/ai-safety-is-extremely-bottlenecked-on-grantmakers), and it’s only the largest of many funders.

The growth isn’t over: AI companies are likely to fuel a new wave of philanthropy. Nan Ransohoff [estimates](https://nanransohoff.substack.com/p/the-third-wave-of-american-philanthropy) that Anthropic staff and the OpenAI Foundation could represent $37–100 billion in _annual_ philanthropic spending once those companies go public.[2](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-2) If even a small fraction of this goes towards AI safety (a concern for [hundreds of people](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/ai-companies-want-the-governments) at both companies), the field will have billions of additional dollars to spend each year.

![Image 1: A chart showing a forecast of rising philanthropy from AI companies, their staff, and Good Ventures.](https://80000hours.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Giving-Chart-large-font.png)

A [Giving Atlas](https://givingatlas.org/giving/overview.html#ai-wave) forecast of charitable giving in all areas from AI companies and their staff in the coming years, relative to Good Ventures (Coefficient’s primary funder).

That money could change how the world prepares for the rise of transformative AI — but only if it reaches impactful projects. Coefficient’s grantmakers [routinely](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/mopsmd3JELJRyTTty/ozzie-gooen-s-shortform?commentId=fms5fr9y7aJpgcNqi)[report](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/B6d8Wzk4gNzHsXvdi/ai-safety-is-extremely-bottlenecked-on-grantmakers) that staff capacity limits how much they give. We’ve heard the same from other major funders. To seize the coming opportunity, AI safety will need dozens of new grantmakers. **If you become one of them, you could direct tens or hundreds of millions of dollars towards highly impactful projects.**

## Why work on grantmaking for AI safety?

The rise of transformative AI may create [dire challenges](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/) for humanity. As Luke Muehlhauser, a managing director at Coefficient, [puts it](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/B6d8Wzk4gNzHsXvdi/ai-safety-is-extremely-bottlenecked-on-grantmakers):

> This pace of technological change is unprecedented, and the world is not prepared. Very little of the commercial, government, and nonprofit infrastructure we need to respond to these transformative changes has been built.

To create this infrastructure, we’ll need skilled founders with good ideas. But good ideas don’t get funded automatically: someone has to bet on the right combination of idea + team. In the startup world, that’s a venture capitalist. In the nonprofit world, it’s a grantmaker.

Much like the best VCs, the best grantmakers go beyond funding; they also use their experience to help grantees improve their plans and make important connections. This takes a rare set of skills: domain expertise, an eye for talent, and the strategic judgment to find the essential features of a complex proposal. Sometimes, they’ll devise a proposal themselves, and look for someone who can make it happen.

Most organisations on our [job board](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?jb_source=career-reviews__ai-safety-grantmaking) are largely funded by grants. So are we. A specific person had to review and sign off on all of those grants. It’s not the most high-profile job, but without it, AI safety would be a fraction of its current size. The field is a chaotic mix of researchers, wonks, and founders, working across hundreds of projects; grantmakers are in a unique position to see the big picture, and to shape strategy for the field as a whole.

Here’s more on why we recommend grantmaking:

### There simply aren’t enough grantmakers

It’s hard to know exactly how much philanthropic funding has gone into AI safety. But our best guess is that the total was under $5 billion as of mid-2026.[3](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-3)

If Nan Ransohoff is right, the field could see that much funding _every year_ once corporate giving kicks off in earnest. But even if annual giving only doubles from its 2026 levels, that will still create demand for dozens of new grantmakers. We were inspired to write this profile because several funders told us they were worried about finding enough people to manage the oncoming tide.[4](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-4)

### Your work can have extremely high leverage

VCs and grantmakers make similar bets: startups and nonprofits can both multiply the value of their funding. Coefficient Giving, one of the world’s largest grantmakers, [aims to generate](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/cost-effectiveness/#0-how-we-measure-impact) at least a 2,000x “social return on investment” (SROI) — meaning that every dollar it spends helps people over 2,000 times as much as a dollar given to someone earning $50,000 a year.

Coefficient has already given over $6 billion to causes that it judged to be above that bar.[5](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-5) For example, it was the first major philanthropic supporter of [David Baker](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/how-neil-king-and-david-baker-are-using-ai-to-create-more-effective-vaccines/) (who later won the Nobel Prize for his work on protein design), and organised a [fund](https://coefficientgiving.org/funds/lead-exposure-action-fund/) that drastically increased global philanthropic spending to mitigate lead poisoning. And there are many other cases where grants generated massive SROI — like the Rockefeller Foundation’s support for agricultural research that enabled the [Green Revolution](https://www.philanthropyroundtable.org/almanac/averting-millions-of-deaths-by-starvation/), or Katharine McCormick’s funding for [contraceptive research](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/04/03/obituaries/katharine-mccormick-overlooked.html) that led to the birth control pill.[6](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-6)

While AI safety grants are often hard to judge, much of the field’s most influential work (from [AI 2027](https://ai-2027.com/) to [METR’s task completion graph](https://metr.org/time-horizons/) to [the campaign that stopped a moratorium on state-level AI regulations](https://archive.is/0pKd1)) relies on philanthropic support. So do the capacity-building projects that made the field’s growth possible (from the [MATS fellowship](https://www.matsprogram.org/) to [BlueDot Impact](https://bluedot.org/)). If you read mainstream news coverage of an alarming development in AI, you’ll probably see a quote from someone whose work is grant-supported.[7](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-7)

Grants also help people develop skills they’ll eventually use elsewhere. When governments began to worry about the impact of transformative AI, they set up [AI safety institutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_safety_institute) — which meant finding hundreds of people with technical governance experience who would choose public service over lucrative corporate jobs. Unsurprisingly, many of those people came from the nonprofit sector, and originally built their experience through grant-supported fellowships or research programmes.

#### What about marginal impact?

You might accept that grants can be very impactful, but still question the value of additional grantmakers. Would you make a difference on the margin, or would your chosen projects attract funding even without you?

The second isn’t as likely as it seems. [Philanthropy isn’t an efficient market](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/open-philanthropy-is-now-coefficient-giving/#1-why-philanthropy-isnt-an-efficient-market). Many opportunities are hard to spot, and a chance that looks promising to you might otherwise go unnoticed.

That said, [adverse selection](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/sWMwGNgpzPn7X9oSk/select-examples-of-adverse-selection-in-longtermist) is a real problem. Some proposals you find may have been passed over for good reasons, and part of your job is to work out whether that happened (and whether you agree with the funders who passed).

Even if another funder says yes eventually, they might be too late: by the time they find the project, its window of opportunity might close, or the founder might give up and take a job elsewhere. And if a project does survive the wait, it could still have had much more impact with an earlier start, especially if we [don’t have much time](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/what-the-hell-happened-with-agi-timelines-453) before the advent of AGI.

Catherine Brewer, an associate program officer at Coefficient Giving, describes a case where timing mattered: Coefficient gave seed funding to a pair of researchers who were leaving a major lab, which enabled them to launch a new organisation. “Had we gone slower or had less grantmaker capacity, it’s likely this grant wouldn’t have happened; they both had other offers.”

It’s easy to assume that grantmakers spend as much as they can, with funding as the ultimate bottleneck. But that’s not true; spending is often limited by staff capacity. Here’s [Luke Muehlhauser](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/B6d8Wzk4gNzHsXvdi/ai-safety-is-extremely-bottlenecked-on-grantmakers) again:

> As a new AI grantmaker at [Coefficient], you’d likely move >$30 million, and plausibly >$100 million, in your first year […] Because grant investigation capacity is tight, hiring one fewer grantmaker usually means those millions will just sit in an account for another year rather than being deployed.

If you deploy tens of millions of dollars that would otherwise go unspent, that buys a lot of chances to find good ideas others won’t — and a [single big hit](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/hits-based-giving/) could more than pay for the rest of your bets.[8](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-8)

### You can help your grantees do more good

Beyond the money itself, you can provide crucial advice and connections to founders who need them.

I’ve heard from grantmakers who changed a grantee’s trajectory by:

**Helping them find employees, board members, or even co-founders.** Alex Lawsen, a senior program officer at Coefficient, said he’d done a “decent amount of targeted headhunting, especially for board roles.” Another grantmaker once made an international trip to pitch a researcher on leaving his corporate job to help run an AI safety org — and succeeded.

**Providing career advice.** Lawsen noted that his job helped him learn about a wide range of organisations, which positioned him to give a “neutral, balanced perspective” to people figuring out their next steps. (Many grants in AI safety go to help individuals develop their career plans, a stage at which they’ll want advice.)

**Encouraging them to be more ambitious.** Julian Hazell, head of AI strategy at the Astralis Foundation, noticed that fellowships and other talent development programmes had a strong track record in AI safety, and thought the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS) was well-placed to run one focused on practical policy skills. He suggested that IAPS branch out from research to launch a fellowship. IAPS had considered this before, but Julian’s advice and grant (from Coefficient Giving, his previous employer) tipped the scale and led them to [act on the idea](https://www.iaps.ai/fellowship).

**Connecting them with helpful experts.** Many would-be grantees have limited experience outside their fields — picture a professor starting a pressure group or a programmer pivoting to policy. You’ll be well-positioned to spot these limitations, and you can draw from your network to connect grantees with advisors who shore up their weaknesses. One grantmaker I’ve worked with helped a first-time CEO find a performance coach to develop their professional skills; another set up media training for a researcher whose work was attracting journalists.

### The job can be highly fulfilling

Here’s what I’ve heard from grantmakers about their favourite parts of the job:

**You really feel the impact you make.** Funding a person or project has an obvious effect on what happens next — and if the grant goes well, you can share in the excitement. Hazell: “You spend all this time evaluating someone, making a bet on them, and then they actually go do the thing. That’s really satisfying.”

**There’s room for individual expression.** Grantmakers — even early in their careers — have lots of flexibility and autonomy to pursue the opportunities they view as most promising. You’ll be asked to form your own views and ultimately make the call (usually with approval from senior staff) on where to allocate millions of dollars.[9](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-9)

**The job is always changing.** You’ll constantly meet new people, evaluate new proposals, and deal with new developments in your field. A single RFP might give you 500 projects to consider.

**You can see the field from the inside.** Alex Lawsen explained that while board membership might expose you to one organisation’s inner workings — the problems they face, the way their leaders make decisions — grantmaking could do this for 10 organisations at once: “It’s hard to overstate how unique a picture [of the field] you get from this.”

You’ll also get time with senior researchers and policy experts who don’t have major public profiles and would be hard to reach otherwise. Catherine Brewer called this “a really fun part of the job, which I underrated before joining.”

## What do grantmakers actually do?

Before you fund someone, you need to find them. In most grantmaking roles, you’ll spend much of your time tracking down potential founders, not just waiting until they come to you. This could include:

*   Searching for leads at conferences and other events.
*   Generating ideas for projects and organisations you’d like to see, then finding people to create them. (Julian Hazell did a version of this when he realised that IAPS was well-positioned to provide policy training.)
*   Writing [requests for proposals](https://www.longview.org/request-for-proposals-on-extreme-power-concentration/) (RFPs) to explain what you’d like to fund, and sharing them with as many relevant groups as you can.
*   Reading the latest work in your field to spot people with interesting ideas, then asking what they’d do with a million dollars. (The actual number varies.)

After you source a proposal, you decide whether to make a grant. This entails:

*   **Assessing the cost-effectiveness of the grant.** While [back-of-the-envelope calculations](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/how-we-use-back-of-the-envelope-calculations-in-our-grantmaking/) (BOTECs) are common in some sectors of impact-focused grantmaking, AI safety tends to be less quantitative. Most of the time, you’ll use some combination of personal heuristics, gut feeling, conversations with your peers, and the outcome of similar grants in the past. That said, BOTECs can still help you with sub-problems, like estimating the attendance of a conference you might fund or the chance that a bill gets through Congress.
*   **Evaluating the people involved.** Do they have the right mix of experience and ability to run the project well? Are their ideas sensible, with a clear theory of change? Would you need to supervise them closely, taking time away from other grants you could make? How should you handle negative information about them?
    *   Here’s an example which blends a few real-world cases: If an applicant’s last project fell apart because they screamed at their subordinates, but they went to anger management training and seem to get along with their current team, would you still apply a risk penalty to their proposal? If you did fund them, how would you monitor the situation?

*   **Deciding whether to impose conditions.** Are you willing to make an unrestricted grant? Will you fund only a subset of the grantee’s work? Will you guarantee additional funding if they hit certain milestones? Will you fund the team, but for a separate project entirely?

You’ll get much of your information from the applicants themselves. But since they may skew the data to improve their chances, you’ll also seek out other sources, like people who worked closely with them or neutral experts who can judge their output.

Once you’ve made a grant, you’ll keep in touch with the grantee for scheduled check-ins and ad hoc advice. This is very flexible; you might talk to someone once a year, or every other week.

Beyond direct grantmaking, the job has many other responsibilities. You’ll set broad strategic priorities, keep up with developments in your field, write about your work, and answer questions from people who seek out your expertise.[10](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-10)

## Could you be a good fit?

### Skills that will help you succeed

**Experience in relevant areas.** To judge a proposal, you must evaluate:

1.   The project itself (how impactful would it be with good execution?)
2.   The people involved (how well do you think they’ll execute?)

On the first point, you’ll need enough background in the right area(s) to gauge a project’s potential: Does the idea make sense? Have similar projects succeeded or failed in the past? Does the proposal address the likely obstacles?

Relevant experience could include national security, technology policy, cybersecurity, machine learning, China, or many other topics in AI safety. If you’ve worked in any of our [priority careers](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/), that’s a good sign.

**Good judgment about people.** Being a domain expert helps you evaluate plans, but isn’t as helpful for evaluating people. That skill is harder to pin down, but here are some positive signals:

*   You’ve hired people before, and they were highly successful in their roles.
*   You’ve recommended contacts for jobs or introduced them to collaborators on several occasions, and seen it work out well.
*   You have a history of picking the right people to build teams or partnerships, in professional or competitive settings.

Some “people judgment” involves universal traits: deciding whether a team seems competent and well-organised, or charismatic and likeable if the work demands it. Some of it requires background knowledge: evaluating a researcher’s technical chops, or whether a think tank’s founder has the right experience and bearing to make politicians take them seriously.

(One comment I’ve heard a lot: “I don’t think this person would come across well on Capitol Hill.”)

**Learning new things quickly.** No matter how experienced you are, grantmaking will force you to contend with new ideas and unfamiliar domains. Julian Hazell’s work has involved crash courses in:

*   “Talent bottlenecks and hiring frictions in the EU.”
*   “The basics of US tort law and how state supreme courts shape it.”
*   “Incentives, frictions, and blockers that labs face around monitoring and tracking what their models are doing in deployment.”

Ideally, you’ll use your first research pass to generate questions for someone who knows more. Grantmakers often meet with experts who help them understand proposals and resolve uncertainties. The trouble is that your experts won’t always agree — so you’ll need enough context and judgment to figure out whose opinion you trust, or come up with the right synthesis.

**Strong communication and [reasoning transparency](https://coefficientgiving.org/research/reasoning-transparency/).** This is important for most jobs, but a few common situations in grantmaking really emphasise it:

*   Writing for colleagues, especially whoever approves your grants. Making your cruxes and the strength of your evidence explicit lets them sign off quickly, or push back for the right reasons.
*   Persuading funders to support an opportunity. In some roles, you’ll need to get approval directly from your funder(s). Compared to your colleagues, they’ll typically have less context on the space and place more weight on whether a grant excites them personally (though funders vary widely on these factors). That means you’ll need to make an especially clear and legible case for each grant, drawing out what makes the work interesting without exaggerating its potential.
*   Delivering feedback to people who aren’t ready to hear it. I’ve heard several stories along the lines of “I tried to tell a grantee they weren’t doing well, but they were shocked when I didn’t renew their funding. I wish I’d gotten my point across better.”

**An extensive information environment.** Alex Lawsen has [written](https://lawsen.substack.com/p/more-on-deferral) that a strong grantmaker can “track every adjacent effort, notice persistent gaps, compare five proposals trying to solve nearby problems, or work out which two groups should probably be talking to each other.”

This goes beyond experience: You’ll need to constantly absorb new information about the space, so that you can discover projects that might benefit from funding or recognise when a sensible-sounding idea no longer makes sense. This involves a mix of networking and reading, depending on how information flows through your part of the field.

**Speed and responsiveness.** Grantmaking is time-sensitive. Someone who requests funding could be choosing between their grant and a full-time job; getting back to them a week sooner might change which path they take. One grantmaker described his work as searching for whichever information might cause him to say no the fastest, so that he could focus on the strongest proposals instead of stringing along potential grantees.

### Promising background experience

Apart from experience in our [priority careers](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/), it helps to have experience:

*   Actually making grants, or providing other forms of support to individuals or small teams (e.g. startup investing, working at a government funding agency like DARPA or NIH)
*   Helping people refine their plans in other contexts (e.g. consulting, coaching)
*   Studying the landscape of AI safety, biosecurity, or related subfields, especially if you built a strong network along the way (e.g. journalism, event organising, research management)
*   Evaluating AI safety work, even on an amateur basis (e.g. writing comments on LessWrong, blogging about research papers, creating BOTECs for your personal donations)

## Downsides to working on grantmaking

**The field can be difficult to enter.** Grantmaking doesn’t have many formal training opportunities, and even entry-level roles are hard to get. Funders struggle to hire because they have high standards for who they’ll trust to make millions of dollars in grants. To quote Ollie Rodriguez (formerly of Longview Philanthropy), “[grantmaking is more like a skill than a path](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/qJfRFkBLDJqyBmz3Q/grantmaking-is-more-like-a-skill-than-a-path)“. To become a strong candidate, you’ll need to build experience and abilities in other positions.

**High stakes beget high pressure.** You can’t fund every proposal you see, but every decision has consequences. If you don’t fund a project, it might not happen; if you don’t renew a grant to an organisation, people might lose their jobs. Meanwhile, if a project you fund goes poorly, you may feel like you’ve wasted a huge amount of someone else’s money — or worse, enabled something actively counterproductive.[11](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-11)

**Your impact is indirect.** You can provide support and guidance to your grantees, but you ultimately won’t have much influence over how most of your grants perform. Some people come to miss “on-the-ground” work where their efforts have direct returns. Ironically, grantmaking also gives you many chances to notice gaps you could fill, if only you were willing to take a new job; several of my sources found this stressful.

**Your work won’t be especially visible.** You’ll spend a lot of time reasoning privately with your colleagues and doing sensitive research you can’t publish. This makes it hard to build a portfolio, or develop career capital that will transfer outside of AI safety. One grantmaker noted another consequence: “You’re not going to get social credit for a lot of the good stuff you do.”

**You may be constrained by your funders.** Grantmakers give away other people’s money. The funders you work with might override your decisions, or impose restrictions that stop you from supporting some of your favourite projects. This can happen even in longstanding relationships, as when Good Ventures [stopped funding](https://web.archive.org/web/20240816060108/https://www.goodventures.org/blog/an-update-from-good-ventures/) some of Coefficient’s sub-causes.[12](http://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking#fn-12)

**Power dynamics distort communication.** When life-changing amounts of money are involved, it’s hard to keep things honest. Applicants might stretch the truth in a proposal or flatter you with empty compliments. As one grantmaker said: “It can be hard to believe positive feedback or signals of respect, because you’re not sure how much of it comes from your position of power.”

Power also changes the way people hear your words: applicants may bend over backwards to give you what you want, even if you don’t feel strongly about a suggestion. You’ll have to communicate carefully to ensure your passing thoughts aren’t taken as conditions for funding.

## Top organisations

These funders work on problems we see as [top priorities](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/).

*   [Coefficient Giving](https://coefficientgiving.org/), the largest grantmaker working on our priority problems
*   [OpenAI Foundation](https://openaifoundation.org/), which has massive resources and an [“AI Resilience” program](https://openaifoundation.org/news/resilience-in-the-age-of-ai) focused on risk mitigation
*   [Effective Altruism Funds](https://funds.effectivealtruism.org/), which just opened its Transformative AI Fund
*   [Longview Philanthropy](https://www.longview.org/), which advises a number of large donors on AI, biosecurity, and nuclear weapons policy
*   [Founders Pledge](https://www.founderspledge.com/), which recommends funding opportunities to its network of entrepreneurs
*   [The Astralis Foundation](https://astralisfoundation.org/), which focuses on European and Asian AI policy alongside other neglected interventions
*   [The Future of Life Foundation](https://flf.org/), whose focuses include [using AI to improve decision-making](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/ai-enhanced-decision-making/)
*   [Lightcone Commons](https://www.lightconecommons.com/), which connects groups of funders with expert evaluators they’ve sourced
*   [Macroscopic Ventures](https://macroscopic.org/), which works on both traditional AI governance and a few unusual initiatives (AI welfare and cooperative AI)
*   [Halcyon Futures](https://halcyonfutures.org/), which makes investments and incubates new organisations in addition to making grants
*   [Sentinel Bio](https://sentinelbio.org/), which works exclusively on biosecurity (a topic that is [highly relevant](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/preventing-catastrophic-pandemics/#:~:text=AI%20progress%20may%20be%20increasing%20catastrophic%20biorisk) to risks from advanced AI)
*   [Schmidt Sciences](https://www.schmidtsciences.org/focus-area-ai/), a science funder that funds occasional AI safety projects

## How to enter the field

Because you can enter grantmaking from a variety of backgrounds, our strongest recommendation is to **[check the grantmaking roles on our job board](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-grantmaking/#find-jobs-in-ai-safety-grantmaking)** and apply if you see a role that fits. While there’s a high bar for entry, your qualifications might be more relevant than you think — and the need is urgent.

More ideas:

*   **Start with a different role in the space.** You’ll need a substantial base of AI safety knowledge to qualify for most grantmaking positions — the kind you’d get from actually working on a job or research project. Even a part-time role can be helpful, especially if it involves evaluating projects (e.g. cost-effectiveness researcher) or helping a grantmaker in some capacity (e.g. research or executive assistant).
*   **If you’re an expert on something else, build AI safety context.** If you have highly relevant skills or experience — grantmaker at a major foundation, cybersecurity expert — you may be a strong candidate even without a formal background in AI safety. However, you’ll still need to know the basics. Good ways to start include courses from [BlueDot Impact](https://bluedot.org/) and our primer on [helping advanced AI go well](https://80000hours.org/ai/guide/summary/).
*   **Study how grantmakers operate.** Funders and individual grantmakers often have blogs, mailing lists, or Twitter accounts. Some, like [Effective Altruism Funds](https://funds.effectivealtruism.org/), publish reports on their funding decisions. I used to write for Coefficient, and I can testify that reading its [blog](https://coefficientgiving.org/research-and-news/) would teach you a lot about its approach (and make you a stronger candidate).
*   **Practice thinking like a grantmaker.** You probably don’t have millions of dollars to give away, but you could still challenge yourself by informally evaluating organisations or projects. For example, Michael Dickens writes about his personal giving in [great detail](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/posts/AGcny8oBxBDCjqxdr/where-i-am-donating-in-2025). This kind of side project can help you [grab a hiring manager’s attention](https://80000hours.substack.com/p/how-to-become-a-better-applicant).
    *   Another idea: Look at payout reports from [Effective Altruism Funds](https://funds.effectivealtruism.org/) and ask yourself how you’d evaluate some of those grants. What questions would you ask before renewing, or to gauge the impact of someone’s work?

*   **Look for training opportunities.** We haven’t heard of many opportunities specific to grantmaking, but they do exist. Ambitious Impact’s [Impactful Philanthropy](https://www.charityentrepreneurship.com/philanthropy-round) programme trains people in multiple philanthropic skills (including grantmaking and advising wealthy individuals), and Constellation’s [Astra Fellowship](https://constellation.org/programs/astra) has included strategy and governance projects linked to grantmaking.

title: The Remarkable Lives of 5-Year-Old Brain Organoids
content:
Our brains are staggeringly complex, which makes studying them difficult. Animal models don’t always faithfully replicate their functions, and researchers can’t go around taking samples from humans, so what’s a neuroscientist to do?

Featured Video

Use cerebral organoids—cultured balls of cells that more closely mimic human brain tissue.

These mini-brains are cultivated from embryonic stem cells, chemically nudged to transform into neural tissue and given three dimensions to grow. In a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10877-x) in _Nature_, scientists are documenting how they develop in the fourth dimension: time.

Most brain organoids are cultured for specific experimental purposes (ranging from studying the neurodevelopmental impacts of [Zika virus](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aaf6116) to [playing _Pong_](https://www.bbc.com/news/science-environment-63195653)). Once they’ve served those purposes, they’re discarded. Now, an international team of scientists has kept them living, growing, and maturing for five years and counting.

**Read more: “[What the Tiny Cluster of Brain Cells in My Lab Are Telling Me](https://nautil.us/what-the-tiny-cluster-of-brain-cells-in-my-lab-are-telling-me-246650)”**

Along the way, they had to come up with new culture media to support the brain organoids’ burgeoning neuronal activity. They then sampled the tissues at different points in time to see how they were progressing, and found the same kind of developmental markers expected from normal human brains. Different cell types appeared in the appropriate order, the complexity of neural connections increased, and their genes switched on and off at predictable times.

In fact, after their first “birthday,” researchers observed milestones that normally only occur postnatally. “The cells are outside the body, yet they still follow approximately the same developmental timeline as we do—and even more closely than we’d anticipated,” study author Noelia Antón-Bolaños of Utrecht University said in a [statement](https://research.umcutrecht.nl/news/brain-organoids-survive-and-mature-for-over-5-years-years/). Not bad for a disembodied mini-brain.

The team also discovered that more mature brain cells maintained some kind of developmental “memory” (distinct from the conceptual memory our complete brains are capable of; these organoids aren’t complex enough for that yet, most likely). When they mixed older organoid cells with younger ones, the resulting chimera was capable of producing new neurons, ones that appeared more mature.

“When we dissociated an older organoid and allowed the cells to grow again, they produced the cell types associated with a late developmental stage,” Antón-Bolaños explained. “Yet when we combined older cells with younger cells, the older cells regained the ability to produce neurons—but only the types associated with later stages of development.”

It’s an exciting finding. Our brains owe their complexity in part to their relatively delayed development. Unlike many other mammals, we emerge from the womb unable to feed ourselves, walk, or even hold our heads upright. Now these more seasoned organoids can shed light on what happens inside our brains during our slow burn to brilliance. ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Are You in Danger of Becoming a Robot?
content:
Humans have been performing robot behavior for laughs for at least a century. In the 1936 film _Modern Times_, Charlie Chaplin [played](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6n9ESFJTnHs) a worker who got stuck in factory mode after he left the assembly line, pulling every lever, pushing every button, and twisting every wheel and bolt he saw involuntarily. In the 1960s, the robot dance motored onto dance floors, with its stilted, angular movements and dime stops. Today, [robot dances](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z_T81uUeZcM) saturate popular culture and social media: K-pop performances lean into the robot aesthetic, with mechanical choreography, glitchy visual effects and futuristic outfits, and variations of robot dance have [taken off](https://www.tiktok.com/discover/the-robot-dance-song) on TikTok. Some of the performances are so convincing it’s tough to know whether you’re watching a human or a machine.

Featured Video

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6n9ESFJTnHs)

_Credit: Charlie Chaplin / YouTube_

But the threat of transformation may be more real than we realize. If humans spend too much time connecting with robots, they may start to resemble them in important ways, according to new [research](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-026-03299-w) from the United Kingdom and Scandinavia. The authors of a study in the journal _AI & Society_ propose that when humans interact repeatedly with AI systems that are designed to feel social—particularly chatbots, service robots, and other personal assistants—they may start reshaping themselves to make it easier for a machine or an algorithm to understand them. They call this existential drift “robotoid humanness.” Over time, they say, it could result in a shift not just in communication style but in identity.

“The risk is not that people will mistake bots for humans, and not that anyone is turning into a robot,” writes study author Inci Toral-Manson, professor of marketing at Birmingham Business School in the U.K., in an email. “It’s quieter than that. It’s that we slowly adjust ourselves to fit what AI can handle.”

Social bots are already a big part of the lives of many Americans. In the United States, recent surveys found that just over half of adults and about two-thirds of teens had used a chatbot like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Copilot. And about a third of adults and teens use large language models about once a day. A tiny fraction of teens, about 4 percent, use them “almost constantly.” But it’s less about frequency than about quality, according to Toral-Manson. “Someone who asks a chatbot 20 questions a day about train times is in a very different position from someone who talks to one every night about how their day went,” she says. “The first is using a tool. The second is doing something closer to a relationship, and that’s where the effect we describe would likely show up.”

The danger lies in the way social bots are built to reward humans over repeated encounters with “frictionless alignment,” Toral-Manson and her colleagues argue. The feedback we get from these bots is fundamentally different from the kind we get from humans, because humans are messy, unpredictable, and will disagree with you, helping you to grow and reconsider who you are, they write. AI systems, on the other hand, are built to be predictable and keep you engaged. “Where human interlocutors furnish heterogeneous and contestable evidence, algorithmic feedback is engineered to converge,” they argue.

**Read more: “[What’s Wrong with Having an AI Friend?](https://nautil.us/whats-wrong-with-having-an-ai-friend-1238214)”**

There are three sets of conditions that will accelerate the mirroring between humans and bots, according to their framework. One is that as algorithmic systems increasingly anticipate what consumers want, they will push a future that’s statistically continuous with the past, reducing the space for actual choice. Second is that if consumers increasingly allow AI to take over writing emails, bios, applications, and dating profiles, they’ll give up authorship over their own lives, creating a larger and more jarring gap between the public self that circulates online and the internal self. And the third is what they call pseudo-intimacy: affirmation on demand disguised as reciprocity. “The consumer is effectively pulled into an interaction that feels like a relationship, which raises the stakes of interpretation, trust, and self-presentation,” they explain.

Toral-Manson sees early signs that people are shaping themselves to fit their interactions with chatbots. “People change how they speak to a voice assistant,” she says. “They write job applications for the software that screens CVs rather than for a person. Writers now avoid certain words and punctuation marks so they won’t be mistaken for a chatbot.” The people most vulnerable to loss of identity and agency are the ones most exposed to social bots, says Toral-Manson: People who are lonely, unwell, very young, or having a hard time. “Something warm and attentive that’s available at 3 in the morning and never gets bored of you isn’t a trivial thing to be offered.”

Toral-Manson and her team ground their account in one of the leading cognitive science frameworks for understanding conscious experience called “predictive processing.” That account holds that rather than passively receiving sensory input, the brain is constantly generating expectations about the world and itself and matching sensory impressions against those expectations. According to predictive processing, the self isn’t stable. It’s relational, always being revised as predictions shift, and developing through social encounters that provide “recognition, resistance, and evaluative feedback.”

While the paper is theoretical, the scientists suggest ways to test their theory. They propose experiments that would measure whether, over repeated conversations with AI, people unconsciously begin to adjust how they express themselves, becoming clearer, more consistent, and more predictable. If the proposed theory is correct, these mirroring effects would be strongest when the robots have the most anthropomorphic and social characteristics. Most of all, the team of scientists is sounding the alarm: The more AI saturates daily life, through service industries and beyond, the more we risk a normalization of “reduced personhood.” ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

The ruins of the Bronze Age metropolis sit on the volcanic island of Santorini, in the southern Aegean Sea, some 120 miles southeast of the mainland. Excavations began in earnest on the island in 1967, and on Aug. 19, 1969, the city was uncovered in its entirety—frozen in time, as Pompeii would be thousands of years later, by a thick coating of pumice and ash.

That pumice and ash came from a giant eruption that archaeologists think happened sometime in the 16th century B.C. While there’s no exact date for it, we know it was one of the largest volcanic eruptions in history—devastating many settlements of the Minoan civilization, including Akrotiri.

The volcanic blanketing of the city has preserved it in remarkable detail. Frescoes, figurines, pottery, furniture, and other artifacts have all been recovered from the site. What hasn’t been found are any skeletons, a distinct difference from Pompeii, suggesting that residents got advance warning of the volcanic eruption—perhaps through earthquakes and tremors—and escaped just in time.

title: Dolphins Eavesdrop on Their Prey—and Each Other
content:
Dolphins are a noisy bunch. They whistle to identify each other and interact socially. And their series of rapid-fire echolocating clicks allow them to feel their way around, acoustically checking out the contours of the underwater landscape and finding prey. These days, however, dolphins have to compete with a ton of different human-made noises, from oil drilling to ship traffic to explosives, that [impair their communication](https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(22)02000-0).

Featured Video

Adding to the acoustic melee, [a paper](https://peerj.com/articles/21547/) recently published in _PeerJ_ found that dolphins may be eavesdropping on fishes that make sound, such as drums (Sciaenidae) that croak by vibrating their swim bladders but are known to [become quieter in the presence of dolphin sounds](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/faf.12612).

Florida Atlantic University researchers with the [Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute](https://www.fau.edu/hboi/) listened in on dolphins for two months along the Atlantic Coast from Fort Pierce to Jacksonville. A wave glider towed an underwater recording device suspended 4 to 10 meters below the surface, while also measuring currents, depths, and other physical parameters.

**Read more: “[What Do Dolphins Talk About?](https://nautil.us/what-do-dolphins-talk-about-238544)”**

In 62 hours of ocean sounds compiled from 15-second recordings every five minutes, dolphins were detected either whistling or echolocating (or both) about 1,700 times. The acoustic data, when crossed with aspects of the physical surroundings, revealed nuances in dolphin sound production. The study paves the way for identifying areas of high acoustic importance to dolphins that should be protected from human noise pollution.

“When we combine dolphin vocalizations with the sounds of their prey and the physical characteristics of the ocean,” explained marine biologist and co-author Greg O-Corry-Crowe in a [statement](https://www.fau.edu/newsdesk/articles/snooping-on-dolphins-acoustic-study), “we begin to see the underwater environment from the dolphins’ perspective.”

They found that dolphins whistled more when close to shore, varying with water temperature and chlorophyll concentrations, among other factors. Because dolphin whistles may carry 12 miles or more, they’re useful in keeping a group together. Their echolocation clicks, on the other hand, were concentrated in two stretches where sound-producing fish are known to abound, including croakers, toadfish, and carangids. And so, the dolphins may be listening to the croaking and other fish sounds to home in on their prey.

“What we’re seeing is a fascinating separation between the acoustic behaviors dolphins use for social life and those they use for finding food,” said O-Corry-Crowe. “Everybody is snooping on everybody else.” ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# AI Can See Optical Illusions

And it might teach us about our own brains

[JC](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](http://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

9:00 AM CDT on August 21, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/08/Currie_HERO_8f7146.png?w=2880)

Long ago, back when twirling things was both an entertaining diversion and a serious mode of scientific inquiry, several researchers noticed an odd optical illusion. Spinning a white disk with a series of black lines produced colors where there weren’t any. A toymaker named Charles Benham turned the optical illusion into a toy, and Benham's Top was born. You can try it for yourself below.

Featured Video

[Video 4](http://nautil.us/ai-can-see-optical-illusions-1284064)

[Video 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/08/Black_CCW_30_e8cb9c.mp4)

_Credit: Laboratory of Neurophysiology / NIBB_

Over the past 200 years, scientists have continued investigating this bizarre phenomenon (now termed “subjective color”), but it’s still somewhat mysterious. The best working theory for subjective color is that it comes from feedback in our visual cortex. Our eyes feed information forward into our brains, but our brains aren’t just sitting there waiting, they’re anticipating and predicting information to fill in the gaps. It’s this feedback that results in seeing colors in moving black-and-white images ([fMRI studies](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20413448/) seem to back up this model).

After two centuries fiddling around with the Benham’s Top illusion, scientists have uncovered several strange idiosyncrasies. For starters, arcs positioned at different distances can evoke different colors, and the colors can reverse when the direction reverses. But what’s even weirder is that artificial intelligence networks can see the Benham’s Top optical illusion too, according to a new [study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-57953-w).

Advertisement

**Read more: “[The Illusion Machine That Teaches Us How We See](https://nautil.us/the-illusion-machine-that-teaches-us-how-we-see-235154)”**

Researchers from the ​​National Institute for Basic Biology in Japan developed an artificial neural network (ANN) designed to predict “what image will come next” and spit out a visual representation. They trained their ANN on a series of first-person videos of natural landscapes (for example, video shot on a head-mounted GoPro from someone taking a relaxing hike). These videos, researchers say, give the network the same sort of visual training input a real person might have.

After the training, they showed their ANN Benham’s Top, and the images it produced also included faint colors. In fact, when they tweaked the spinning disk to move the arcs or reverse the direction, the ANN “saw” the same things a human would.

According to the team, the artificial neural network had learned to work in the same way our biological neural networks do. Because rapidly moving objects are especially challenging for the ANN to predict, they have an outsized impact during its training. The result is a “visual cortex” that works remarkably like our own, complete with the same feedback. Basically, it’s more confirmation for the feedback model of subjective color.

title: Why Human Giants Defy the Laws of Physics
content:
According to legend, giants once roamed the Earth. In Homer’s _Odyssey_, Odysseus encounters the Cyclops, the one-eyed son of Poseidon, living in a huge cavern, hungry and angry. He grasps men and sheep in one hand, devouring them whole. In the days of King Arthur, a clever young boy earned the title of “Jack the Giant Killer,” using his sharp wit to outsmart and slay the various “giants” plaguing the land. Another Jack—or perhaps it is the same Jack—famously plants some magic beans and climbs the resulting beanstalk to a castle in the clouds, cleverly outwitting the giant residing there.

Featured Video

All these giants of legend have a humanoid form, and they undertake generally human activities—walking, stomping, dancing, carrying heavy loads, running, and so forth. They act and move about in a human manner, only at a larger scale. But if human giants did exist,[could they actually _survive_ in this form](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yiRx6dvC9jk)?

In his foundational 1638 text _Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences_, Galileo Galilei argues that this folklore understanding of the nature of giants is fundamentally flawed. He contends that this idea of a massive humanlike creature is, quite simply, physically impossible.

To begin his argument, Galileo asks us to imagine a structural beam of sturdy oak. The beam might be used to support a heavy load—perhaps a load of bricks or a great stone.

He then asks us to imagine a much larger oak beam, scaled up in size but with the same proportions and material. A thicker, solid oak beam, of course, will naturally support more than a slender beam of the same wood. But _how_ much more can it support? Will the larger beam be able to support the same load, but also scaled up in size? Should we expect the larger beam to support a scaled-up load of bricks or a scaled-up stone?

Galileo ingeniously argues _no_—the larger beam will not support a similarly scaled-up load. Indeed, he claims that at a certain sufficient scale, the beam will no longer support even its own weight! His argument relies on a certain subtle observation concerning how scaling works in different dimensions.

Galileo first observes that the load-bearing strength of a beam depends on its cross-sectional area, since a failure of the beam involves it breaking across a cross section. Since area scales as the square of the linear factor, a 10-times larger beam—with length, width, and depth each scaled by a factor of 10—will have a cross-sectional area 100 times larger than before. In other words, a 10-times larger beam is 100 times stronger! It will be able to support 100 times the load as the smaller beam.

That may seem initially very good. But the problem is that the weight of the load, for a given material density, is determined by its volume, and volume scales with the _cube_ of the linear factor. Scaling up a load of bricks or a great stone by a linear factor of 10, therefore, will cause a 1,000-fold increase in the volume—a 10-times larger stone weighs 1,000 times more.

Galileo brings these observations to their natural collision. A 10-times-larger beam is 100 times stronger, yes, but the similarly scaled-up load became 1,000 times heavier. If the smaller beam had been carrying the optimal load, therefore, then the scaled-up beam would not be able to support the scaled-up load—not even close! It would support only one-tenth of it. Galileo argues that any given beam will have a certain sufficiently scaled-up size at which it will no longer support even its own weight. The strength of the beam scales with the square, but the mass of the beam itself scales with the cube, so at a sufficient scale, the beam will simply be too heavy for its own strength.

Now back to giants. Picture the bones of a giant serving, in effect, as structural “beams” supporting its body mass, its flesh, and muscles. If the giant’s bones are made of the same stuff as ordinary men, his strength has not scaled the same as his mass.

The conclusion, Galileo writes, is catastrophic for the giant:

_Clearly then if one wishes to maintain in a great giant the same proportion of limb as that found in an ordinary man he must either find a harder and stronger material for making the bones, or he must admit a diminution of strength in comparison with men of medium stature; for if his height be increased inordinately he will fall and be crushed under his own weight._

Similarly, scaled-up versions of wooden ladders would not support a scaled-up giant human climbing them; scaled-up swords would be too heavy for such giants to lift; scaled-up armor would be too heavy to wear; scaled-up wooden houses would not support their own roofs; a scaled-up wooden chair would not support even itself, let alone a giant sitting in it; and scaled-up dining glasses would be too weak to hold the volume of wine or water within them. In short, the entire world of giants as pictured in folklore does not fully make physical sense.

While Galileo’s argument explains the nonexistence of human giants, it also explains the existence of nature. Namely, of animals such as hippopotamuses, rhinoceroses, elephants, and dinosaurs, which tend (or tended) to be stocky, with proportionally thicker, sturdier bones than smaller animals.

Elephants, for example, have much thicker legs relative to their size than do dogs and cats. This is explained by Galileo’s observation that the strength of bones scales with the square of the linear scale, since it depends on the cross-sectional area of the bones (and perhaps the pulling strength of muscles also depends on cross-sectional area), but the weight of the animal scales with the cube. So, the bones themselves need to become proportionally thicker to support the increased weight.

A dual effect occurs when scaling down in size. Very small animals, for example, are typically slender and lithe. Insects tend to have relatively thin limbs, which would be entirely inadequate to support the animal if scaled up proportionally to a much larger size. Unlike humans, small insects can often jump many times their own height. Insects can walk on walls and ceilings—they weigh so little, in fact, that electrostatic forces are strong enough to hold them fast to the surface.

If one were to encounter a fly that was 10-times normal size, but with the same proportions and body design, it would weigh 1,000 times as much, and the tiny electrostatic forces would be insufficient to allow it to stick to walls. It would certainly not be able to fly, and probably it could not even support itself standing on those toothpick legs. Water bugs can walk on the surface of water, because at that scale, the surface tension of the water is proportionally strong enough to support the meager mass, but larger bugs would be too heavy. The laws of physics and the basic nature of chemical and physical reality simply do not scale uniformly with size.

Galileo’s paradox applies just as much to the folklore conception of the miniature human, such as with the Lilliputians or the Hollywood films _Downsizing_, _Ant-Man_, or _Honey, I Shrunk the Kids!_ The Lilliputians of _Gulliver’s Travels_, for instance, are about six inches tall, and the bones of such a 10-times scaled-down human would be 100 times weaker, while weighing 1,000 times less. Such a person would therefore not walk about normally but could probably jump very high (relative to his or her height) and carry correspondingly huge loads. For example, at normal size, a human can often carry another human on his or her back, but not much more. But the one-tenth-size humans, as Galileo notes, would be able to carry much more:

_Whereas, if the size of a body be diminished, the strength of that body is not diminished in the same proportion; indeed the smaller the body the greater its relative strength. Thus a small dog could probably carry on his back two or three dogs of his own size; but I believe that a horse could not carry even one of his own size._

Meanwhile, however, the tiny humans would find themselves subject to all manner of forces that are more prominent at small scale. They would stick to walls and other things more easily because of the electrostatic forces, and water would be a big problem, seeming much stickier at small scale. In short, the folklore vision of Lilliputians or other tiny humans walking about as humans ordinarily do is fundamentally flawed and ultimately just as physically impossible as giants are.

Galileo’s observations enable us to see easily how evolutionary forces might work on body size. Perhaps for some organisms, there are comparatively few genes that control the overall body size in such a way that the typical size of an animal will be subject to evolutionary forces of natural selection.

We have clear evidence of species of animals greatly changing in size over evolutionary time scales. Early mammals were very small. For example, horses used to be about the size of small dogs—and a vestige of this can be seen today in the miniature horse breeds. Many insects, by contrast, were larger. Before dinosaurs and birds, dragonflies had wingspans of several feet, while we’ve found fossils of cockroaches up to four inches long. But the body shapes are not simply scaled exactly up and down. Evolutionary forces have acted on these body-size plans over time to improve survival, performing an optimizing arbitrage for the comparative advantages available in each size.

Galileo glimpsed a subtle, secret aspect of our physical existence: He perceived the core dimensional nature of important features such as strength and mass, realizing as a purely mathematical consequence that these features will therefore scale differently in those different dimensions. So despite the enormous range of sizes available in the physical universe, our lives would not be the same at a different scale. Giants are impossible. The Lilliputians are to be found only in literature. And as for humans, there is a very good reason we are the size we are. ![Image 1](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Your Book Review: A Residence Of 21 Years In The Sandwich Islands
content:
[_This is one of the finalists in the 2026 book review contest, written by an ACX reader who will remain anonymous until after voting is done. I’ll be posting about one of these a week for several months. When you’ve read them all, I’ll ask you to vote for a favorite, so remember which ones you liked_]

In October 1819, my grandmother’s grandfather’s grandfather, Hiram Bingham I, stood with his wife, Sybil, and his friends outside Park Street Church in Boston and bade farewell to family before venturing into the unknown. They would spend the next five months on a cramped ship sailing to a foreign land of strange people, full of “destitution, degradation, and barbarism.” They did not know if they would ever return to America.

Unlike others who voyaged out to sea, they were not whalers, nor merchants trying to make a quick profit. Instead, their goal was far more ambitious: to uplift an entire nation out of heathenry to civilization. Or as Hiram wrote, to “most effectually and most extensively promote the Redeemer’s cause with the means that are put into our hands”.

I first came across Hiram’s memoir, _A Residence of Twenty-One Years in the Sandwich Islands_, on my honeymoon to the Hawaiian Islands last summer. I had vague knowledge of a family connection to the area, and decided to do some research into it. As I started reading, I had a growing sense of _deja vu_ as I recognized my own patterns of thinking in Hiram’s words.

Today’s Effective Altruists sincerely want to do the most good possible, and often focus on international development as a means of improving lives. However, there is another group who fits that description equally well: 19th-century missionaries.

Hiram and his colleagues believed that Heaven and Hell were not metaphorical, and that doing the most good meant saving the most souls from eternal torment. And what, they asked themselves, was the most effective means towards accomplishing this goal? Spreading the Gospel to those who had never heard it. All of humanity required salvation, and those who lived in foreign lands mattered just as much as those who lived nearby.

As a missionary destination, the Hawaiian Islands (then known as the Sandwich Islands), had several compelling advantages. First, the islands were very neglected, being recently discovered. While not as important as China, Egypt/Palestine, or India, they still held a sizable population. And unlike those places, there was little competition from other missionaries or pre-existing organized religions, making them much more tractable for conversion. The mission to Hawaii would prove notably cost-effective compared to other missions[1](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-1). Basically all that was needed was a ship, a printing press, and missionaries to teach the Bible.

In other words, if the EA Forum existed in the early 19th century, I could easily imagine a post arguing that bringing the Gospel to the Sandwich Islands is a promising cause area.

So, with the benefit of 200 years of hindsight, what can Effective Altruists and other aspiring do-gooders today learn from the previous wave of people who wanted to save the world?

To find out, I read Hiram’s memoir, _A Residence of Twenty-One Years in the Sandwich Islands._ Published in 1847, it’s not a particularly engaging book[2](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-2), but as a historical document, it’s a fascinating account of the effort of seven young missionary couples and their Hawaiian friends to do the most good possible by bringing Christianity, literacy, Western civilization, and Puritan social mores to a nation of 130,000 souls.

In many ways, the islands of Hawaii are a paradise on Earth, but to the missionaries who knew them as the Sandwich Islands, they were a savage place. These islanders, after all, had killed [Captain Cook](https://www.britannica.com/biography/James-Cook) just 40 years ago[3](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-3). From 1782 to 1810, the nation was ravaged by war. [King Kamehameha I](https://www.nps.gov/puhe/learn/historyculture/kamehameha.htm), adopting Western military technology such as gunpowder, forcefully unified the islands into a single kingdom and suppressed potential rivals.

A young boy, [Opukaha’ia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Opukahaia), was left an orphan by Kamehameha’s warriors, who killed his father, mother, and infant brother. With nothing left for him in Hawaii, he joined the crew of a passing ship, and eventually made his way to New England, where he converted to Christianity and befriended theology students at Yale and Andover. Opukaha’ia described his native Hawaii as a land in need of salvation, and the local ministers decided to send a mission to spread the Gospel and the light of civilization. Opukaha’ia would return to Hawaii with the missionaries and serve as a translator.

Hiram Bingham, a student at Andover Seminary, heard Opukaha’ia’s call to aid the Hawaiians. Born October 30, 1789, Hiram was one of the thirteen children of a Congregational deacon, Calvin Bingham. Although his parents had wanted Hiram to take over the family farm and care for them in old age, Hiram felt his duty to God was greater, and convinced his parents to allow him to study for the ministry. In Hiram’s own words, “Christ undoubtedly requires all his followers to bear their cross, and to forego or forsake whatever comes in competition with rendering him the highest service”. But service to God was not a gloomy undertaking; instead, it was accomplished “with joyful hearts and grateful praise.”

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FwUp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97c629e2-4632-49da-9cef-8bdc9129c018_2048x1536.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FwUp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F97c629e2-4632-49da-9cef-8bdc9129c018_2048x1536.jpeg)

An old family portrait of Hiram and his six brothers taken sometime 1854-1860. Bottom row: Asa, Amos, Calvin, Luther. Top row: Hiram, Stephen, David. Not pictured were his six sisters.

Hiram truly felt the commandment to “love thy neighbor”, and for him, the 130,000 native Hawaiians on the other side of the globe were neighbors just as much as the inhabitants of his hometown in Vermont. Thus, Hiram was eager to become a missionary as soon as he had finished his studies.

Unfortunately, during preparations for the mission, Opukaha’ia fell ill and died[4](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-4). Still, the plan went ahead. As Hiram writes, a good Christian must “extend the influence of the Gospel, because Christ _requires_ it, rather than because of his own _engagement_. To know, to be qualified, to have opportunity, constitute the special call to do good.” Parents and relatives urged the missionaries not to go, but Hiram saw things differently: somebody had to and no one else would.

There was just one problem: Hiram needed a wife. Sending a young single man to a land of licentious heathens was asking for trouble, and therefore only married couples were allowed to be missionaries. Thus, after being ordained as a Congregational minister, Hiram proposed marriage to Sybil Moseley, a woman he had met at the ordination ceremony just twelve days earlier. Fortunately, she accepted, and later that month, the couple was on a ship bound for Hawaii — not as a two-week honeymoon, but as a mission that would last twenty-one years.

After a sea voyage of 18,000 miles, during which Hiram and Sybil’s first child was conceived, the missionaries spotted the peak of Mauna Kea on the morning of March 30, 1820. Five months after departure, the sight was exhilarating: the work of spreading Christianity, literacy, and civilization was finally at hand.

There was just one important restriction, put in place by the American missionary board: **absolutely no meddling in the politics of the natives**[5](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-5)**.**

Upon arriving, the missionaries’ first request was for an audience with King Kamehameha, the fearsome conqueror of the islands. Kamehameha’s authority upheld the kapu (taboo) system[6](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-6), the foundation of the native Hawaiian religion. Converting him to Christianity would be difficult, but crucial for the success of the mission. Kamehameha’s authority was absolute, and anyone who went against it would be exiled or killed. Unless he converted, the mission was doomed to fail.

However, the missionaries were shocked to find Hawaii in a state of political and religious turmoil. Several months before their arrival, Kamehameha had fallen ill and died. His son and heir, [Liholiho](https://www.nps.gov/puhe/learn/historyculture/kamehameha2.htm), was just 21 years old and inexperienced in politics. [Queen Ka’ahumanu](https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/queen-ka-ahumanu.htm), who had been Kamehameha’s favorite among his many wives[7](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-7), took control. Officially, she was regent in the king’s name, but in practice she ruled Hawaii.

As a woman, Ka’ahumanu was burdened by the many restrictions of the kapu system. Among other things, many foods (such as coconut) were forbidden to women, and women were not allowed to eat together with men. Soon after becoming regent, Ka’ahumanu allied with Kamehameha’s other widows, including Liholiho’s mother, [Queen Keopuolani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ke%C5%8Dp%C5%ABolani), to abolish the kapu, which she “felt to be degrading and oppressive” to herself and the other women of Hawaii.

Conveniently, this also removed some of the customary limits on her power as a queen regent, and boosted her popularity. It seemed that all along, nobody had really liked the kapu. Well, almost nobody: there was a brief insurrection of traditionalists, but this was soon crushed. As the kapu system fell, so too did the native Hawaiian religion.

Thus, the missionaries arrived to find their work half done for them. The Hawaiians themselves had discredited and discarded their former religion. But what was to take its place? A missionary’s nightmare of rum and atheism, or “an elevated state of Christian civilization”?

The intended audience with Kamehameha was impossible, but the missionaries soon met with the Hawaiian royal family, including King Liholiho and Queen Ka’ahumanu. After twelve days of negotiations, during which the missionaries assured the Hawaiians that they were purely benevolent and definitely not looking to meddle in politics or “interfere with the government or trade of the islands”, Ka’ahumanu and Liholiho granted them permission to settle. Half the missionaries, including the expedition co-leader Asa Thurston, would remain on the big island, and the other half (including Hiram) would continue to Honolulu.

From then on, Hiram and his fellow missionaries worked tirelessly to establish “the school, the pulpit, and the press”. The royal family was impressed by their “kindness and demonstration of their ability and readiness to make themselves useful”, and their gifts of a telescope and ornate Bibles[8](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-8). The missionaries were granted a plot of land on which to build a house and a church, and a school was soon added. Although Opukaha’ia had died before the mission departed, the missionaries brought four other native Hawaiians who were able to translate, including Prince George Humehume (the son of Kaumuali’i, chief of Kaua’i), and Hiram quickly learned the language himself.

The native Hawaiians were fascinated by the missionaries’ technology, even for seemingly simple things. Several high-ranking Hawaiian women requested that the missionary wives make American-style dresses for them. In traditional Polynesian culture, obesity is considered a mark of high status, and the missionaries had never seen women that big. Hiram describes one as a “rude giantess”[9](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-9). Some initial attempts at dresses were “too tight” but after alterations, the dresses were well received.

Besides dress-making and other fabric production, the Hawaiians were intrigued by American-style houses. The missionaries brought pre-cut lumber to build a house, which was much more comfortable than the native grass huts: among other advantages, a chimney let smoke escape instead of filling the entire room. Music, and musical instruments, also delighted the Hawaiians, and Hiram adapted several hymns to the native language.

In addition to improving the physical lives of the Hawaiians, these new technologies were a gateway to what Hiram saw as spiritual improvement. Hiram remarked that initially, native Hawaiians “are not able to appreciate [a missionary’s] knowledge of the classics or what is called learning, but they can appreciate the talents of a man who can build a house or make a coat better than they can. By such means a missionary establishes, in their view, his superiority over them. This being done, they will listen to his religious instructions with deference, and feel confidence in him as a teacher.”

But Hiram and his missionaries were not the only Westerners introducing things to the Hawaiians. In 1820, the north Pacific had a large whale population, at a time when the Atlantic whales had declined due to overharvesting. This caused a whaling boom in the region. Many whalers supported the missionaries, but others were a bad influence. They brought rum and spread syphilis and other diseases. Even before Hiram’s visit, some native women were having sex with sailors in exchange for pieces of iron. As Hiram wrote, “That was the dearest bought iron, doubtless, ever bartered for guilty indulgences; and thousands have been the victims of suffering and death, throughout the whole group, as the lamentable consequence of evils thus introduced, and not yet wholly eradicated.”

Alcohol, especially distilled spirits such as rum, were also popular among the Hawaiians. Without any social immunity to alcohol or stigma about drinking, alcoholism was rampant. Foreign merchants repeatedly got the king drunk, then tricked him into making bad trade deals. Most of the sandalwood trees on the islands were cut down to sell the valuable wood. At one point, Hiram intervened when the king was offered a drink: “I gently took the uncorked bottle, and offering it to the earth rather than to his majesty, turned it bottom upwards on the mat.” Although Hiram’s “attempt to thrust aside a deadly weapon” did little to earn the king’s favor, most of the royal women were sympathetic to Hiram’s efforts to keep the king sober.

George Humehume, the Hawaiian prince who had accompanied the missionaries on their journey from Massachusetts back to his native land, also found the temptation of drinking too much to resist. Although Hiram had hoped George would be a key ally due to his high status among Hawaiians, his alcoholism led him to abandon the missionaries. Although Hiram was sad to lose a close friend, he notes that this ended up being a good thing for the mission, because later on, George would become even more disgraceful.

Faced with these difficulties, Hiram almost gave up and moved to Kamchatka in the Russian Far East (what a change of climate!), but heard from the Russians that the native Kamchatkans were all converted already. To Hiram, the Russian Orthodox church was a valid form of Christianity, and “though not in its unobscured glory”, it at least ”engaged in promoting the circulation of the Holy Scriptures”, unlike the “Popes and Jesuits”.

However, the missionaries would soon make an important breakthrough. In December 1821, Queen Ka’ahumanu fell ill with some unnamed disease. The missionaries prayed and cared for her as best they could, and Mrs. Sybil Bingham “sat down by the side of the sick queen, and with unfeigned sympathy for her sufferings and danger, bathed her aching temples, she bound a silken cord around her heart, from which I think she never broke loose while she lived.” Sybil’s compassion won the Queen over to Christianity, and she proved to be an invaluable ally for the missionaries. But King Liholiho, being polygamous, was reluctant to convert, since that would have required him to give up his wives.

Caring for Ka’ahumanu was far from Sybil’s only contribution to the mission. She also ran the school, which “having commenced with ten or a dozen children and adults, now numbered forty regular scholars, attending five or six hours daily”, made garments for the missionaries and any Hawaiians who requested them, led weekly prayer meetings, and managed all aspects of running a respectable household in an unfamiliar climate. Not to mention giving birth to seven children![10](http://www.astralcodexten.com/p/your-book-review-a-residence-of-21#footnote-10)

Meanwhile, Hiram had been hard at work devising a writing system for the Hawaiian language. Others before him had tried, but failed because they didn’t know the language well enough, and wrote things like “Owhyhee” for Hawaii or “Hanaroorah” for Honolulu. If the native Hawaiians remained illiterate, Hiram foresaw a grave danger: Catholicism.

> “[they] might indeed have been taught to cross themselves, repeat Pater Nosters and Ave Marias in Latin, to dip the finger in water, gaze on pictures, bow before images, and buy indulgences with great formality and punctuality, and still have been as ignorant of the volume of inspired truth as the Aborigines of California and South America . . . To make the spelling and reading of the language easy to the people, and convenient to all who use it, was a matter of great importance, almost indispensable to our success in raising the nation.”

To standardize the spelling in a way intended to be easy for native speakers, Hiram set a fixed alphabet of twelve letters: “a, e, i, o, u, h, k, l, m, n, p, w”, with an additional set of consonants for foreign words, “b, d, f, g, r, s, t, v, and z”. There were some differences in local dialects: for example, Hiram writes tabu instead of kapu, since k/t and b/p were interchangeable, as well as r/l and v/w. Hiram’s standardized orthography is still in use today.

January 7, 1822 marked a milestone: the first printing press became operational, and began printing books in Hawaiian for the missionary school. The royalty quickly learned the advantage of sending written communication to administer the kingdom, and native Hawaiian newspapers became popular. In a few years, one third of the population attained a basic level of literacy – a higher proportion than many European countries of the time. Most of these were not taught by the missionaries themselves, but by other Hawaiians who showed great enthusiasm for learning (called _palapala)_. Hawaiians wrote poems in their own language “of no inferior order compared with the ancient Greek and Latin odes”. The missionaries would go on to print nearly 150 million pages (over 1000 for each Hawaiian) over the next 23 years.
